title: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping Blurs Into a Cloud of Drudgery
excerpt: The Hunger Games prequel shows occasional glimmers of life, but in the end it feels like more of the same—only less.
content_html:
Just when you think there’s no more life in a franchise, an executive somewhere puts a crowbar in the crypt and revives an old moneymaker for one more round. The first four Hunger Games movies, released from 2012 to 2015 and adapted from Suzanne Collins’ enormously successful young-adult novels, featured Jennifer Lawrence as the ever-plucky Katniss Everdeen. She gave those movies a bristling vitality that could keep you watching even if you had no interest in the material's hyper-dramatic teen dystopian visions. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping—directed, like all the films in the franchise save the first, by Francis Lawrence—is a prequel to the story told in those earlier films, and though it occasionally shows some glimmers of life, in the end it feels like more of the same, only less. Unless you’re a true fan of the earlier films, 2 hours and 38 minutes of scrappy survivalist tactics, mildly brutal confrontations between teens fighting for survival, and somber pronouncements about democratic values may be 2 hours and 38 minutes too many.

Sunrise on the Reaping is set, like the earlier movies, in the divided futuristic nation of Panem, where the power center known as the Capitol rules over 12 downtrodden districts; every year, two unlucky teenagers from each district are selected to participate in a televised fight-to-the-death battle. Sunrise on the Reaping takes place 24 years before the events of the first Hunger Games film, opening on the 16th birthday of Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), a curly haired swain whom everyone seems to like. That day also happens to be the day the unfortunate Hunger Games contestants, or tributes, are chosen. This year, the 50th edition of the games, is known as the Second Quarter Quell. That means, as the event’s grotesque chairlady Drusilla Sickle (Glenn Close) announces in her trilling, grating voice, four kiddos from each district, two boys and two girls, will be chosen to face off against their peers.

Ostensibly, the tributes are chosen at random. But because Haymitch has principles and stands up for what’s right, angering the jackbooted creeps known as the Peacekeepers, he’s doomed to be chosen to compete. His fellow District 12 tributes are Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang), who believes, possibly wrongly, that brains can beat brawn in these games; little Louella McCoy (Molly McCann), who tries to face her fate bravely in her little homemade dress; and saucy Maysilee Donner (McKenna Grace), a seemingly snobby girl with Daryl Hannah tresses who turns out to be a staunch, loyal ally once the games get under way.

Sunrise on the Reaping isn’t just a prequel; it’s a sequel to another prequel, 2023’s The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, set 10 years earlier. That film outlined the backstory of the young Coriolanus Snow, a not-bad kid who would nonetheless grow up to become the nasty authority figure played by Donald Sutherland in the earlier Hunger Games movies. In Sunrise on the Reaping, Snow is played by Ralph Fiennes: The games begin with the tributes being transported into a large arena on wobbly chariots. Fiennes surveys the scene with check-cashing eyes. Sunrise on the Reaping is yet more evidence that in a difficult movie climate, big franchise films are the best place for acclaimed performers to make a buck when the jobs are scarce. Another old-guard actor, Lili Taylor, also shows up, in a tiny, thankless role. The younger generation is represented by Kieran Culkin as smarmy emcee Caesar Flickerman, Jesse Plemons as showrunner Plutarch Heavensbee, and Elle Fanning as the fluttery wardrobe mistress Effie Trinket, the character played by Elizabeth Banks in the earlier films.   

As the story trundles on, bad stuff happens. People you care about and people you don’t die tastefully unpleasant deaths. There are some admittedly grand visuals here, including an attack by a flock of deadly candy-red birds that pays a chilly homage to The Birds; elsewhere, a cloud of pretty blue butterflies descends around our hero—he’ll learn pretty quickly that they have electrocution capabilities. There’s something sadistic about the scenarios dreamed up by the powerful Capitol creeps to trip up and kill all these poor teenage tributes, who are not only fighting one another, but struggling to survive in an artificial environment that’s designed to kill them. The extremism is the point, probably; it’s ostensibly galvanizing to see a bunch of teenagers valiantly stand up to authoritarianiasm, even when they fail.

Still, the endless bickering and battles blur into a kind of drudgery. The movie gets a jolt of energy from a father-son duo of characters, Kelvin Harrison Jr’s Beetee Latier  and Percy Daggs IV’s Ampert Latier, who seem to have borrowed their style, and their justifiable anger, from 1970s Black revolutionaries. That’s a clever touch, but the movie doesn’t go far enough with it. As Haymitch, the kid who’s determined to change the system, Zada is a pleasing, earnest presence; he’s like a teen Greek god who’s decided, for no good reason, that he prefers being an Earthling. But mostly, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is a jumble of cornpone homilies and sub-Star Trek-level civics lessons, a slog of teenage miserableism that exists just so Woody Harrelson—the man young Haymitch will grow up to be—can finally show up, beaming in a knit beanie, proud of the progress he’s made for District 12 and the suffering underlings of Panem. The ideals here are noble, but instead of taking flight, they hit with a thud.
